newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU drops probe into AC Nielsen /IRI data row. [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EU drops probe into AC Nielsen /IRI data row. [CORRECTED 18:25 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline and text to remove references to Dun & Bradstreet, reflecting fact that AC Nielsen is no longer a subsidiary of Dun & Bradstreet)

The European Commission said on Tuesday it had dropped a probe into allegations that AC Nielsen abused its position in the European market for sales data collection after Nielsen changed its practices.
"Karel Van Miert, the commissioner responsible for competition policy, has obtained an undertaking from AC Nielsen Company to modify its contractual practices," it said in a statement.

The Commission started an investigation in May into a complaint by Information Resources Inc that Nielsen's practices were effectively stopping it from accessing sales data in Europe which is necessary for provinding retail tracking services.
At stake in the dispute between the two firms was the practice by which Nielsen entered into exclusivity contracts with both retailers providing sales data and manufacturers wishing to buy it.

The Commission said Nielsen had commited itself to terminate any restrictions on retailer's freedom to supply data to other companies. Nielsen also agreed to allow multinationals to switch to a competitor in a given country without loosing conditions granted in another country.

The outcome is a victory for Information Resources, which has been attacking Nielsen's worldwide leadership in the market tracking services since it launched the first scanner to register purchases at checkout counters.
The Commission heralded the move as good news for consumer goods giants, such as Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola and Nestle, which need such services to know how their sales evolve.

This also attested of the good co-operation between the EU and the Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice which also closed its own investigation into the case in view of the results achieved in Europe, the Commission said.

Nielsen's commitments are only valid for a period of three years, however, due to the dynanimc nature of the market, the Commission said. The company will submit periodic reports to enable the EU's competition watchdog to monitor the situation. -- Brussels newsroom 322 2876841
